title: Theorem
body_md:
Let $\mathscr{C}$ be a locally presentable, closed symmetric monoidal category.
Let $F\colon \mathscr{C}\rightarrow \mathscr{C}$ be an accessible, lax symmetric monoidal functor. 
Then the category of $F$-algebras in $\mathscr{C}$ is enriched, tensored and cotensored over the closed symmetric monoidal category of $F$-coalgebras in $\mathscr{C}$.

name: {\cref{thm:enriched}}

label: thm: alg enriched in coalg
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm: alg enriched in coalg}
The category $\mathrm{Alg}_k$ of $k$-algebras is enriched in the closed symmetric monoidal category $(\mathrm{coAlg}_k, \otimes_k, k, \underline{\mathrm{coAlg}}_k(-,-))$ of $k$-coalgebras, for which the hom-coalgebra between two algebras $A$ and $B$ is given by the universal measuring $\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}_k(A, B)$. 
It is also tensored over $\mathrm{coAlg}_k$ via the measuring tensor and cotensored via the convolution algebra. In other words, we obtain the following natural isomorphisms in $\mathrm{coAlg}_k$:
\[
\underline{\mathrm{coAlg}}_k(C, \underline{\mathrm{Alg}}_k(A, B))\cong \underline{\mathrm{Alg}}_k(C\triangleright A, B) \cong \underline{\mathrm{Alg}}_k(A, [C,B]).
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The convolution algebra $[-,-]\colon \mathrm{coAlg}_k^\mathrm{op}\times \mathrm{Alg}_k \rightarrow \mathrm{Alg}_k$ determines $\mathrm{Alg}_k$ as a right module over $\mathrm{coAlg}_k^\mathrm{op}$, in the sense that we have the following natural isomorphisms in $\mathrm{Alg}_k$ for all coalgebras $C,D$ and algebra $A$
 \[
 [C\otimes_k D, A]\cong [C, [D,A]] \quad \quad [k, A]\cong A.
 \]
 Thus $\mathrm{Alg}_k^\mathrm{op}$ is a left module over $\mathrm{coAlg}_k$ via $[-,-]^\mathrm{op}\colon \mathrm{coAlg}_k\times \mathrm{Alg}_k^\mathrm{op}\rightarrow \mathrm{Alg}_k^\mathrm{op}$.
 Moreover, for any algebra $B$, the induced functor $[-,B]^\mathrm{op}\colon \mathrm{coAlg}_k\rightarrow \mathrm{Alg}_k^\mathrm{op}$ has a right adjoint $\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}_k(-, B)\colon \mathrm{Alg}_k^\mathrm{op}\rightarrow \mathrm{coAlg}_k$ as we have the natural isomorphism
 \[
 \mathrm{coAlg}_k(C, \underline{\mathrm{Alg}}_k(A, B))\cong \mathrm{Alg}_k(A, [C, B]). 
 \]
 By \cite[3.1]{hylandetal}, we obtain that $\mathrm{Alg}_k^\mathrm{op}$ is enriched, tensored and cotensored over $\mathrm{coAlg}_k$.
 Thus $\mathrm{Alg}_k$ is enriched, tensored and cotensored over $\mathrm{coAlg}_k$.

title: Theorem
body_md:
Consider a category $\mathscr{C}$ with a terminal object $1$ and limits of sequences $\omega \to \mathscr{C}$, where $\omega$ denotes the countably infinite ordinal. Consider an endofunctor $F$ that preserves these limits. Then the limit of the following sequence is a terminal coalgebra of $F$:
    \[ \cdots \to F^2 1 \xrightarrow{F !} F 1 \xrightarrow{!} 1. \]

title: Proof
body_md:
For (1), asking that $\alpha$ restricts to a map $\alpha_Q$ is exactly asking that $(Q, \alpha_Q)$ is an algebra of $F$ and that the quotient map constitutes a total algebra homomorphism $q\colon (A, \alpha) \to (Q, \alpha_Q)$. 
        Since the forgetful functor $\mathrm{Alg} \to \mathscr{C}$ is faithful, it reflects epimorphisms. The second statement (2) is immediate.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For (1), consider $\iota \colon S \rightarrowtail C$. Asking that $\chi$ restricts to a morphism $\chi_S$ means exactly that $\iota$ constitutes a total algebra homomorphism $\iota \colon (S, \chi_C) \to (C, \chi)$. This is a monomorphism since the forgetful functor $U\colon \mathrm{Alg} \to \mathscr{C}$ is faithful and thus reflects monomorphisms.

    For (2), consider a monomorphism $\iota\colon(S, \chi_S) \rightarrowtail (C, \chi)$. In order to show that $\iota \colon S \to C$ is also a monomorphism, consider two points $x, y\colon1 \to S$ in $\mathscr{C}$ such that $\iota x = \iota y$. Since $\mathscr{C}$ is assumed to be well-pointed, it suffices to show that $x = y$. Note that $\llbracket{x}\rrbracket = \llbracket{\iota x}\rrbracket = \llbracket{\iota y}\rrbracket =  \llbracket{y}\rrbracket$, and let $((I, \chi_I), \top_n)$ denote a coalgebra generated by a point of this index. Then we get two maps $\overline x, \overline y\colon(I, \chi_I) \to (S, \chi_S)$ and a map $\overline{\iota x} = \overline{\iota y} \colon (I, \chi_I) \to (C, \chi)$ such that $\iota \overline x = \overline{\iota x} = \overline{\iota y} = \iota \overline y$. Since $\iota$ is a monomorphism, $\overline x = \overline y$, but then $x = \overline x \top_n = \overline y \top_n = y\colon * \to \mathscr{C}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first claim that ${\mathrm{Alg}}(A, [C,B])$ is empty or a singleton for any coalgebra $C$.
    Since $!_A\colon \mathbb N \to A$ is an epimorphism, the function
    \[{\mathrm{Alg}}(A, [C,B]) \xrightarrow{!^*_A}  {\mathrm{Alg}}(\mathbb N, [C,B]) \]
    is an injection, and since $\mathbb N$ is initial, ${\mathrm{Alg}}(\mathbb N, [C,B]) \cong *$.
    Thus, ${\mathrm{Alg}}(A, [C,B])$ is a singleton, in the case where the only map $\mathbb N \to [C,B]$ factors through $A$, and otherwise is empty.

    We now claim that the canonical map $\llbracket{-}\rrbracket\colon{\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,B) \to {\mathbb N_\infty}$ is a monomorphism. Suppose there are maps $a,b\colon C \to {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,B)$ from a coalgebra $C$ such that $\llbracket{a}\rrbracket = \llbracket{b}\rrbracket$. Recall that the coalgebra ${\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,B)$ is defined by the following universal property for any coalgebra $C$
    \[ {\mathrm{coAlg}}(C,{\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,B)) \cong {\mathrm{Alg}}(A, [C,B]).\]
    Thus, ${\mathrm{coAlg}}(C,{\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,B))$ is a singleton, so $a = b$, and $\llbracket{-}\rrbracket$ is monic.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose $(C, \chi_C)$ and $(D, \chi_D)$ are coalgebras. Then $C\otimes D$ has the following coalgebra structure:
    \[
\begin{tikzcd}
{C \otimes D} \ar{r}{\chi_C \otimes \chi_D} & [1em] {F(C) \otimes F(D)} \ar{r}{\nabla_{C,D}} & {F(C\otimes D).}
\end{tikzcd}
\]
The morphism $\eta\colon \mathbb I\rightarrow F(\mathbb I)$ provides the coalgebraic structure on $\mathbb I$.

To see that $({\mathrm{coAlg}}, \otimes, (\mathbb I, \eta))$ is a symmetric monoidal category, we first need to check that $(C, \chi_C)\otimes (\mathbb I, \eta)\cong (C, \chi_C)$. On objects, we have $C\otimes \mathbb I\cong C$ as $\mathbb I$ is a monoidal unit. The coalgebraic structures correspond as we have the following commutative diagram by unitality of $(F, \nabla, \eta)$:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
   C \ar{r}{\cong}\ar{d}[swap]{\chi} & C\otimes \mathbb I \ar{dr}{\chi\otimes \eta} \\
   F(C) \ar[bend right=2em, equals]{rrrr} \ar{r}{\cong} & F(C)\otimes \mathbb I \ar{r}[swap]{\mathrm{id}\otimes \eta}& F(C)\otimes F(\mathbb I) \ar{r}{\nabla} & F(C\otimes \mathbb I)\ar{r}{\cong}  & F(C).
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Similarly, we have a natural isomorphism $ (\mathbb I, \eta)\otimes (C, \chi_C)\cong (C, \chi_C)$ from the identification $\mathbb I\otimes C\cong C$. 
Moreover, we also have the following natural isomorphism
\[
((C, \chi)\otimes (C', \chi')) \otimes (C'', \chi'') \cong (C, \chi)\otimes ((C', \chi') \otimes (C'', \chi'')),
\]
lifted from $(C\otimes C')\otimes C''\cong C\otimes (C'\otimes C'')$.
Lastly, the symmetry $C\otimes C'\cong C'\otimes C$ lifts to ${\mathrm{coAlg}}$. Therefore as $\mathscr{C}$ is symmetric monoidal, the above natural identifications assemble to a symmetric monoidal structure on ${\mathrm{coAlg}}$ as the pentagon, triangle, hexagon and symmetric identities remain valid in ${\mathrm{coAlg}}$.

Suppose now that $\mathscr{C}$ is locally presentable and closed, and $F$ is accessible. Then for all objects $X\in \mathscr{C}$, we have that $X\otimes -\colon \mathscr{C}\rightarrow \mathscr{C}$ is a left adjoint functor,  with right adjoint given by its the internal hom $[X, -]\colon \mathscr{C}\rightarrow \mathscr{C}$. 
Since $\mathrm{coAlg}$ is also locally presentable and colimits are computed in $\mathscr{C}$, we get that for all $C\in \mathrm{coAlg}$, the induced functor $C\otimes -\colon \mathrm{coAlg}\rightarrow \mathrm{coAlg}$ also preserves all colimits and thus must be a left adjoint as $\mathrm{coAlg}$ is locally presentable. 
We denote by $\underline{\mathrm{coAlg}}(C,-)\colon \mathrm{coAlg}\rightarrow \mathrm{coAlg}$ its right adjoint. The construction is natural in $C$ and thus defines the desired closed structure on $\mathrm{coAlg}$.

label: thm:enriched
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:enriched}
Suppose that $\mathscr{C}$ is a locally presentable, symmetric monoidal closed category. Let $F\colon \mathscr{C} \to \mathscr{C} $ be an accessible lax symmetric monoidal endofunctor.
Then the category ${\mathrm{Alg}}$ is enriched, tensored, and cotensored over the closed symmetric monoidal category ${\mathrm{coAlg}}$ respectively via
\[
{\mathrm{Alg}}^\mathrm{op} \times {\mathrm{Alg}}\xrightarrow{{\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(-,-)} {\mathrm{coAlg}}, \quad {\mathrm{coAlg}}\times {\mathrm{Alg}} \xrightarrow{-\triangleright-} {\mathrm{Alg}}, \quad {\mathrm{coAlg}}^\mathrm{op}\times {\mathrm{Alg}}\xrightarrow{[-,-]} {\mathrm{Alg}}.
\]
In other words, for any coalgebra $C$, and algebras $A$ and $B$, we obtain the natural identifications in $\mathrm{coAlg}$:
\[
  \underline{\mathrm{coAlg}}(C, {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,B))\cong {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(C \triangleright A, B) \cong {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A, [C, B]).  
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The convolution algebra functor $[-,-]\colon{\mathrm{coAlg}}^\mathrm{op}\times {\mathrm{Alg}}\rightarrow {\mathrm{Alg}}$ presents ${\mathrm{Alg}}$ as a right module over ${\mathrm{coAlg}}^\mathrm{op}$. 
    Thus ${\mathrm{Alg}}^\mathrm{op}$ is a left module over ${\mathrm{coAlg}}$ via \[[-,-]^\mathrm{op}\colon {\mathrm{coAlg}}\times {\mathrm{Alg}}^\mathrm{op} \rightarrow {\mathrm{Alg}}^\mathrm{op}.\] 
    Moreover, for any $A\in {\mathrm{Alg}}$, the functor $[-,B]^\mathrm{op}\colon{\mathrm{coAlg}}\rightarrow {\mathrm{Alg}}^\mathrm{op}$ 
    has a right adjoint ${\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(-, B)\colon{\mathrm{Alg}}^\mathrm{op}\rightarrow {\mathrm{coAlg}}$ as shown in \cref{remark: universal measuring as an adjoint}.
    Thus, by \cite[3.1]{hylandetal}, the category ${\mathrm{Alg}}^\mathrm{op}$ is enriched over ${\mathrm{coAlg}}$ with tensor $[-,-]^\mathrm{op}$. 
    Therefore ${\mathrm{Alg}}$ is enriched over ${\mathrm{coAlg}}$ with power $[-,-]$.

label: thm: most general
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm: most general}
    Let $\mathscr{C}$ be a locally presentably and closed symmetric monoidal category.
    Let $F,G\colon \mathscr{C}\to \mathscr{C}$ be accessible endofunctors.
    Assume that $F$ is lax symmetric monoidal, and that $G$ is an $F$-module, in the sense that there is a transformation
    \[ FX \otimes GY \to G( X \otimes Y) \]
    natural in $X,Y$ and satisfying the diagrams of \cite[Def.~39]{yetter}.
Then the category ${\mathrm{Alg}}_{G}$ is enriched, tensored and cotensored over ${\mathrm{coAlg}}_F$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We obtain a convolution algebra ${\mathrm{coAlg}}_F^\mathrm{op} \times {\mathrm{Alg}}_{G} \to {\mathrm{Alg}}_{G}$ by taking a coalgebra $(C,\chi)$ and an algebra $(A, \alpha)$ to the following composite
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
    G[C,A] \ar{r} & {[FC, GA]} \ar{r}{\chi^*} \ar{r} & {[C, FA]} \ar{r}{\alpha_*} & {[C,A]},
\end{tikzcd}    
\]
    where
    the unmarked arrow is the adjunct of the following composite
    \[
    \begin{tikzcd} 
    FC\otimes G([C,A]) \ar{r} & G(C\otimes [C,A]) \ar{r}{G(\mathrm{ev})} & GA
\end{tikzcd}  
    \]
    where $\mathrm{ev}$ denotes evaluation. The action on morphisms is given by the naturality of constituent arrows of this constructed algebra structure. The functoriality is inherited from the functoriality of $[-, -]$. 

    The diagrams of \cite[Def.~39]{yetter} exactly correspond to the opposite 
    \[[-,-]^\mathrm{op} \colon {\mathrm{coAlg}}_F \times {\mathrm{Alg}}_{G}^\mathrm{op} \to {\mathrm{Alg}}_{G}^\mathrm{op},\]
     this functor being a left action in the sense of \cite{hylandetal}.
    Since $[-,A]^\mathrm{op}$ preserves colimits, so does $[-,A]^\mathrm{op} \colon {\mathrm{coAlg}}_F \to {\mathrm{Alg}}_{G}^\mathrm{op}$. Since ${\mathrm{coAlg}}_F$ is locally presentable, and $\mathrm{Alg}_G^\mathrm{op}$ is essentially small, the functor has a right adjoint.
    Thus, by \cite[Prop.~3.1]{hylandetal}, we see that ${\mathrm{Alg}}_{G}^\mathrm{op}$ is enriched, tensored and cotensored in ${\mathrm{coAlg}}_F$. Thus, ${\mathrm{Alg}}_{G}$ is enriched, tensored and cotensored in ${\mathrm{coAlg}}_F$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
To apply previous result, we only need to show there exists an $F$-module structure on $GF$, that is, we need a certain natural map 
    \[ FX \otimes GFY \to GF( X \otimes Y). \]
    The $\mathscr{C}$-enrichment of $G$ produces a map $X \otimes GY \rightarrow G(X\otimes Y)$ for any objects $X$ and $Y$ in $\mathscr{C}$. Indeed, this is the adjunct of
    \[
    \begin{tikzcd}
        X \ar{r} & {[Y, X\otimes Y]} \ar{r} & {[GY, G(X\otimes Y)]},
    \end{tikzcd}    
    \]
    where the first map is the coevaluation of the internal hom, and the second map is induced by the $\mathscr{C}$-enrichment. We apply this map to $FX$ and $FY$ to get the following composition
    \[ FX \otimes GFY \rightarrow G(FX\otimes FY) \xrightarrow{G \nabla} GF (X \otimes Y).\]
    One can check that this makes the diagrams of \cite[Def.~39]{yetter} commute.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We consider an object $\lim^C\mathrm{id}_{\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}$ with the following universal property:
\[ {\mathrm{Alg}}(A,{\lim}^C\mathrm{id}_{\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}) \cong \lim_{X \in {\mathrm{Alg}}} \ {\mathrm{coAlg}} (C, {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,X)).  \]
(This is the limit of $\mathrm{id}_{\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}$ weighted by the constant functor at $C$.)
Since the hom ${\mathrm{coAlg}} (C, {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,-))$ preserves limits and $\lim_{X \in {\mathrm{Alg}}} X \cong \mathbb N$, we have
\begin{align*}
    \lim_{X \in {\mathrm{Alg}}} \ {\mathrm{coAlg}} (C, {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,X)) &\cong {\mathrm{coAlg}} (C, {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,\lim_{X \in {\mathrm{Alg}}} X)) \\
    &\cong {\mathrm{coAlg}} (C, {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,\mathbb N)) \\
    &\cong {\mathrm{Alg}}(A, [C,\mathbb N]) \\
    &= {\mathrm{Alg}}(A, C^*).
\end{align*}
Thus, $C^*$ has the universal property of $\lim^C\mathrm{id}_{\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}$.

Note that for any $C$-initial algebra $A$, we have $\lim_{X \in {\mathrm{Alg}}} \ {\mathrm{coAlg}} (C, {\underline{\mathrm{Alg}}}(A,X))$ is the terminal object. Thus, by this universal property of $C^*$, there is a unique map $A \to C^*$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider the coalgebra morphism $m \colon (\mathbb{n}-1)^\circ \to \mathbb{n}^\circ, i \mapsto i$.
    This induces a morphism
    \begin{align*}
        m\triangleright A \colon (\mathbb{n}-1)^\circ \triangleright A &\to  \mathbb{n}^\circ \triangleright A \\
        [n,i,a] &\mapsto [n,i,a].
    \end{align*}
    This morphism is monomorphic by definition.
    Since $A$ is $\mathbb{n}^\circ$-initial, we know $\mathbb{n} \triangleright A$ is an initial object.
    This means $m\triangleright A $ is a monomorphism into the initial object, hence an isomorphism.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $k\leq n$.
    Define the coalgebra morphism
    \begin{align*}
        p_j \colon \mathbb{k}^\circ &\to \mathbb{n}^\circ \times \mathbb{n}^\circ \\
        i &\mapsto (i,i+j)
    \end{align*}
    for all $0 \leq j \leq n-k$.
    Consider the composition of measurings $\varphi \circ (\mathrm{id} \times -_{A} \circ \varphi) \in \mu_{\mathbb{n}^\circ \times \mathbb{n}^\circ}(A,\mathbb N)$.
    We can precompose this measuring with the coalgebra morphism $p_j$ to obtain a measuring
    $$
    \mathbb{k}^\circ \times A \xrightarrow{p_j \times \mathrm{id}_A} \mathbb{n}^\circ \times \mathbb{n}^\circ \times A \xrightarrow{\varphi \circ (\mathrm{id} \times -_{A} \circ \varphi)} \mathbb N.
    $$
    We also have the coalgebra morphism $f\colon \mathbb{k}^\circ  \to \mathbb{n}^\circ, i \mapsto i$ which we can precompose with $\varphi$.
    This gives us a measuring
    $$
    \mathbb{k}^\circ \times A \xrightarrow{f \times \mathrm{id}_A} \mathbb{n}^\circ \times A \xrightarrow{\varphi} \mathbb N.
    $$  
    Since $A$ is also $\mathbb{k}^\circ$-initial, we know these measurings must coincide.
    Hence we can state
    $
    \varphi(i,a) = \varphi(i,-_{A} \circ \varphi(i+j,a))
    $
    for all $i \in \mathbb{k}^\circ$ and $0 \leq j \leq n-k$.
    The only restriction placed on $k$ was that $k \leq n$.
    Iterating over all $0 \leq k \leq n$, we arrive at the desired result
    $$
    \varphi(i,a) = \varphi(i,-_{A}\circ \varphi(i+j,a))
    $$
    for all $0 \leq i \leq n$ and $0 \leq j \leq n-i$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\varphi(i,a) = \varphi(i, (\varphi(i, a))_A)$ by the previous lemma, we know
    $
    [0,i,a] = [0, i, (\varphi(i, a))_A]
    $
    in $\mathbb{n}^\circ \triangleright A$.
    We also have $[\varphi(i,a),z] = [0,i,a]$, and by definition of the equivalence relation $\sim$, we have
    $
    [0, i, (\varphi(i, a))_A] = [\min(i, \varphi(i, a)), z].
    $
    From this we conclude
    $$
    \varphi(i,a) = \min(i, \varphi(i, a)),
    $$
    hence $\varphi(i,a) \leq i$ for all $i \in \mathbb{n}^\circ$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We proceed by induction over $k$.
    For $k = 0$, we have that $\mathbb{k} \cong 1$, the terminal object in the category of algebras.
    Hence $\varphi_0 : A \to 1$ is an algebra morphism.
    For the inductive step, assume $\varphi_{k-1} : A \to \mathbb{k}-1$ is an algebra morphism.
    We wish to show $\alpha_k(\varphi_k(a)) = \varphi_k(\alpha(a))$ for all $a \in A$.
    If $\varphi_k(a) = 0$, we know
    \begin{align*}
         \varphi(k,\alpha(a)) & = 1 + \varphi(k-1,a) \\
         &= 1 + \varphi(k-1, (\varphi(k,a))_A) \\
         & = 1 + \varphi(k-1, 0_A) \\
         &  = 1 = \alpha_k(0) \\
         &= \alpha_k(\varphi(k,a)).
    \end{align*}
    If $\varphi_k(a) \geq 0$ we can make the following deduction
    \begin{align*}
        \alpha_k(\varphi_k(a)) 
        &= \alpha_k(\varphi(k, a))\\
        &= 1 + \alpha_{k-1}(\varphi(k,a) - 1)\\
        &= 1 + \alpha_{k-1}(\varphi(k,(\varphi(k,a)) - 1)_A)\\
        &= 1 + \alpha_{k-1}(\varphi(k-1,(\varphi(k,a) - 1)_A))\\
        &= 1 + \varphi(k-1,  \varphi(k,a)_A)\\
        &= 1 + \varphi(k-1, a)\\
        &= \varphi(k,\alpha(a)).
    \end{align*}

title: Proof
body_md:
By \cref{prop:map from initial alg to dual}, there exists a unique morphism $A \to [\mathbb{n}^\circ, \mathbb N]$ for any $\mathbb{n}^\circ$-initial algebra $A$.
    Since $\mathbb{n}$ is $\mathbb{n}^\circ$-initial we know there exists a unique morphism $m \colon \mathbb{n} \rightarrowtail [\mathbb{n}^\circ, \mathbb N]$.
    Upon closer inspection $m$ turns out to be a monomorphism.
    Given any two morphisms $f,g \colon A \to \mathbb{n}$, we can draw the following diagram
    \[\begin{tikzcd}
        A & {[\mathbb{n}^\circ, \mathbb N]} \\
        & \mathbb{n}
        \arrow["{!}", from=1-1, to=1-2]
        \arrow["f"', shift right, from=1-1, to=2-2]
        \arrow["g", shift left, from=1-1, to=2-2]
        \arrow["m"', tail, from=2-2, to=1-2].
    \end{tikzcd}\]
    Since the morphism $A \to [\mathbb{n}^\circ, \mathbb N]$ is unique, we know the composites $m \circ f = m \circ g$, and by $m$ being mono we conclude $f = g$.
    Hence, there can be at most one algebra morphism from a $\mathbb{n}^\circ$-initial algebra $A$ to $\mathbb{n}$.

title: Theorem
body_md: The algebra $\mathbb{n}$ is the terminal $\mathbb{n}^\circ$-initial algebra.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Given an $\mathbb{n}^\circ$ initial algebra $A$, by Proposition \ref{prop:Atonexists} we obtain an algebra morphism $\varphi_n \colon A \to \mathbb{n}$.
    By Lemma \ref{lem:Atonunique} it is unique.
    We conclude $\mathbb{n}$ is the terminal $\mathbb{n}^\circ$-initial algebra.

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider the coalgebra morphism $\iota\colon S_{M,n-1}^\circ \to S_{M,n}^\circ, s \mapsto s$.
    This induces a morphism
    \begin{align*}
        \iota\triangleright A \colon S_{M,n-1}^\circ \triangleright A &\to  S_{M,n}^\circ \triangleright A \\
        [e_{\operatorname{Fr}}] &\mapsto [e_{\operatorname{Fr}}]\\
        [s,a] &\mapsto [s,a]\\
        [m,\ell] &\mapsto [m, \mathtt{map}(\iota \triangleright A)(\ell)].
    \end{align*}
    This morphism is monomorphic by definition.
    Since $A$ is $S_{M,n}^\circ$-initial, we know $S_{M,n} \triangleright A$ is an initial object.
    This means $\iota\triangleright A $ is a monomorphism into the initial object, hence an isomorphism.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $k\leq n$.
    First, we define a function which takes two trees and appends the second tree to all the roots of the first tree.
    We define it as
    \begin{align*}
        (++) \colon S_{M,\infty} \times S_{M,\infty} &\to S_{M,\infty} \\
        (e_S, s) &\mapsto s\\
        ((m, \ell), s) &\mapsto (m, \mathtt{map}( (++) s )(\ell)).
    \end{align*}
    For all $0 \leq j \leq n-k$, define the coalgebra morphism
    \begin{align*}
        p_j\colon S_{M,k}^\circ &\to S_{M,n}^\circ \times S_{M,n}^\circ \\
        s &\mapsto (s,\widetilde{s} ++ s_j),
    \end{align*}
    where $\widetilde{s}$ is the unique tree $\widetilde{s} \in S_{\{e\}, k}$ such that $\mathtt{shape}(\widetilde{s}) = \mathtt{shape}(s)$.
                                              
    Consider the composition of measurings $\varphi \circ (\mathrm{id} \times  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A} \circ \varphi) \in \mu_{S_{M,n}^\circ \times S_{M,n}^\circ}(A,S_{M})$.
    We can precompose this measuring with the coalgebra morphism $p_j$ to obtain a measuring
    $$
    S_{M,k}^\circ \times A \xrightarrow{p_j \times \mathrm{id}_A} S_{M,n}^\circ \times S_{M,n}^\circ \times A \xrightarrow{\varphi \circ (\mathrm{id} \times  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A} \circ \varphi)} S_{M}.
    $$
               
    We also have the coalgebra morphism $\iota\colon S_{M,k}^\circ  \to S_{M,n}^\circ, s \mapsto s$ which we can precompose with $\varphi$.
    This gives us a measuring
    $$
    S_{M,k}^\circ \times A \xrightarrow{\iota \times \mathrm{id}_A} S_{M,n}^\circ \times A \xrightarrow{\varphi} S_{M}.
    $$  
    Since $A$ is also $S_{M,k}^\circ$-initial, we know these measurings must coincide.
    Hence we can state
    $
    \varphi(s,a) = \varphi(s, 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A} \circ \varphi(\widetilde{s} ++ s_j,a))
    $
    for all $s \in S_{M,k}^\circ$ and $0 \leq j \leq n-k$.
    The only restriction placed on $k$ was that $k \leq n$.
    Iterating over all $0 \leq k \leq n$, we arrive at the desired result
    $$
    \varphi(s,a) = \varphi(s, 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A}\circ \varphi(\widetilde{s} ++ s_j,a))
    $$
    for all $0 \leq i \leq n$ and $0 \leq j \leq n-i$.
    In particular this holds for $s = s_i$, and noting $s_i ++ s_j = s_{i + j}$ we obtain the desired result.

title: Proof
body_md:
We will proceed by induction over $i$.
    For the base case $i = 0$, we have $s_0 = e_S$, so $\varphi(s_0, a) = e_S \in S_{M,0}$.
    For the induction step, assume $\varphi(s_i, a) \in S_{M,i}$.
    Using $s_{i+1} = (e,(s_i)^{(\infty)})$ and the previous lemma we can write
    $
    \varphi(s_{i+1}, a) = \varphi( (e,(s_i)^{(\infty)}),  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A}(\varphi(s_{i+1}, a))).
    $
    Let $\alpha\colon 1 + M \times (S_M)^{\leq \infty} \to S_M$, then we can write $(m,s) = \alpha^{-1}(\varphi(s_{i+1}, a))$ where $s$ is the list with components $s_i$.
    We then know by definition of a measuring that
    $$
    \varphi(s_{i+1}, a)  = \varphi( (e,(s_i)^{(\infty)}),  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A}(\varphi(s_{i+1}, a))) = 
    (e \bullet m, \mathtt{map}(\varphi)(\mathtt{zip}((s_i)^{(\infty)}, k)   ) ),
    $$
    where $k = \mathtt{map}( 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A})(s)$.
    By the induction hypothesis, we know $$\mathtt{map}(\varphi)(\mathtt{zip}((s_i)^{(\infty)}, k)   )  \in (S_{M,i})^{\leq \infty},$$ hence $\varphi(s_{i+1}, a) \in S_{M,i + 1}$ by definition.
    This concludes the induction step and the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
We proceed by induction over $k$.
    For $k = 0$, we have that $S_{M,k} \cong 1$, the terminal object in $\mathrm{Set}$.
    Hence $\varphi_0\colon A \to S_{M,0}$ is an algebra morphism.
    For the inductive step, assume $\varphi_{k-1}\colon A \to S_{M,k-1}$ is an algebra morphism.
    We wish to show $\varphi_k$ is an algebra morphism.
    In more detail, we aim to show $$\alpha_k(m, \mathtt{map}(\varphi_k)(\ell)) = \varphi_k(\alpha(m,\ell))$$ for all $(m,\ell) \in M \times A^{\leq \infty}$.
    First, we will write $\ell = (a_i)_{i = 0}^j$, where $j \in {\mathbb N_\infty}$.
    We can now write
    \begin{align*}
        \alpha_k(m, \mathtt{map}(\varphi_k)(\ell))
        &= \alpha_k(m, \mathtt{map}(\varphi_k)((a_i)_i))\\
        &= \alpha_k(m, (\varphi_k(a_i))_i)\\
        &= \alpha_k(m, (\varphi_k \circ  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A} \circ \varphi_k(a_i))_i).
    \end{align*}
    Writing $\varphi_k \circ  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A} \circ \varphi_k(a_i) = t_i$, we can make the case distinction
    $$ 
    t_i = 
    \begin{cases}
        e_S &\text{ if } \varphi_k(a_i) = e_S \in S_M \\
        (m_i, \mathtt{map}(\varphi_{k-1} \circ  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A})(a_i)) &\text{ if } \varphi_k(a_i) = (m_i,a_i) \in S_M
    \end{cases}
    $$
    by $\varphi \colon S_{M,n}^\circ \times A \to S_M$ being a measuring.
    This means $$\alpha_k(m, \mathtt{map}(\varphi_k)(\ell)) = \alpha_k(m, (t_i)_i).$$
    By the algebra structure of $S_{M,k}$, we can write this as
    $
    \alpha_k(m, (t_i)_i) = (m,(r_i)_i),
    $
    where
    $$
    r_i = 
    \begin{cases}
        e_S &\text{ if } \varphi_k(a_i) = e_S \in S_M \\
        \alpha_{k-1}(m_i, \mathtt{map}(\varphi_{k-1} \circ  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A})(a_i)) &\text{ if } \varphi_k(a_i) = (m_i,a_i) \in S_M.
    \end{cases}
    $$
    By the induction hypothesis
    $
    \alpha_{k-1}(m_i, \mathtt{map}(\varphi_{k-1} \circ  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A})(a_i)) 
    = (\varphi_{k-1} \circ  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A})(m_i, a_i)
    $
    and we can write
    $$
    r_i = (\varphi_{k-1} \circ  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A})(\varphi_k(a_i)) = (\varphi_{k-1} \circ  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A} \circ \varphi_{k-1})(a_i)
    $$
    using \cref{lem:adddepth}.
    Retracing our steps, we now compute
    \begin{align*}
        \alpha_k(m, \mathtt{map}(\varphi_k)(\ell))
        &= (m,(r_i)_i)\\
        &= (m, (\varphi_{k-1} \circ  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A} \circ \varphi_{k-1})(a_i)_i)\\
        &= (m, \mathtt{map}(\varphi_{k-1}) (( 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A} \circ \varphi_{k-1})(a_i))_i)\\
        &= \varphi_k(\alpha(m,  ( 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A} \circ \varphi_{k-1})(a_i))_i  ))\\
        &= (\varphi_k \circ  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A} \circ \varphi_k)(\alpha(m, (a_i)_i ))\\
        &= \varphi_k(\alpha(m, \ell))
    \end{align*}
    using that $\varphi$ is a measuring twice.
    We conclude $\varphi_k \colon A \to S_{M,k}$ is an algebra morphism for all $0 \leq k \leq n$.

title: Proof
body_md:
By \cref{prop:map from initial alg to dual}, there exists a unique morphism $A \to [S_{M,n}^\circ, S_{M}]$ for any $S_{M,n}^\circ$-initial algebra $A$.
    Since $S_{M,n}$ is $S_{M,n}^\circ$-initial we know there exists a unique morphism $\iota \colon S_{M,n} \rightarrowtail [S_{M,n}^\circ, S_{M}]$.
         
    This map is given by
    \begin{align*}
        \iota \colon S_{M,n} &\to [S_{M,n}^\circ, S_{M}] \\
        e_S &\mapsto \operatorname{const}_{e_S}\\
        (m,\ell) &\mapsto
        \left( 
        s' \mapsto 
        \begin{cases}
            e_S &\text{ if } s' = e_S \\
            (m'\bullet m, \mathtt{map}(\iota)(\mathtt{zip}(\ell,\ell'))) &\text{ if } s' = (m', \ell').
        \end{cases}
        \right).
    \end{align*}
    We can easily conclude $\iota$ is a monomorphism by observing that $\iota(s)(s_n) = s$ for all $s \in S_{M,n}$.
    Given any two morphisms $f,g\colon A \to S_{M,n}$, we can draw the following diagram
    \[\begin{tikzcd}
        A & {[S_{M,n}^\circ, S_{M}]} \\
        & S_{M,n}
        \arrow["{!}", from=1-1, to=1-2]
        \arrow["f"', shift right, from=1-1, to=2-2]
        \arrow["g", shift left, from=1-1, to=2-2]
        \arrow["\iota"', tail, from=2-2, to=1-2].
    \end{tikzcd}\]
    Since the morphism $A \to [S_{M,n}^\circ, S_{M}]$ is unique, we know the composites $\iota \circ f = \iota \circ g$, and by $\iota$ being mono we conclude $f = g$.
    Hence, there can be at most one algebra morphism from a $S_{M,n}^\circ$-initial algebra $A$ to $S_{M,n}$.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md: The algebra $S_{M,n}$ is the terminal $S_{M,n}^\circ$-initial algebra.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Given an $S_{M,n}^\circ$-initial algebra $A$, by  \cref{prop:AtoS_nexists}, we obtain an algebra morphism $\varphi_n \colon A \to S_{M,n}$.
    By \cref{lem:AtoS_nunique}, it is unique.
    We conclude $\mathbb{n}$ is the terminal $S_{M,n}^\circ$-initial algebra.
